title: Date Counter
context: Grade 5, the pages on the days between two dates. An adult sees a subtraction of dates with a sum after it. What the pages are doing is making the child say whether both days are counted, so that a course or a fair counts both, and a date some days after or a fortnight later adds the days without counting the first again.

writeup.why: Count the days from one date to another, counting both days, across a month end as well, find a finish date from a start date and a number of days, and find a date some days after or a fortnight later.
writeup.look: A month calendar, or two months side by side, with a run of shaded day cells, a counter that says whether both end days are included, and a violet jump of days.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Date Counter' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of days counted. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The month calendar fills the left of the area at x 90, y 230, 700 wide, in seven columns each 100 wide, with the dates in rows beneath, each row 64 tall. When a run crosses a month end, two months stand side by side, each 340 wide, with the last day of the first month marked in ink. The start date is set on it in deep blue, labelled Start, and the end date, or the number of days, beside it in deep blue, labelled Given. The days between them are shaded as a run of cells and counted one by one. The day counter stands at x 850, y 240 and says whether the first day and the last day are included. The count is green, labelled Answer, at x 850, y 560, and a last day found is green, labelled End. The Cut handle stands at x 850, y 340 and splits a run at the last day of the first month. A violet jump of days, labelled Jump, is dragged along the calendar from a date, and a jump of 14 days stands for a fortnight. The date being counted is amber. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a delete key, and keys for days and the month names. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the nine tools of this chapter share them. What the question gives, as a clock time, a length of time, a start date or a number of days, is deep blue, labelled Given or Start. What the working reaches, as an end time, a length of time, a converted time or a date, is green, labelled Answer, End or How long. The thin second hand and the seconds it counts are vermilion, labelled Second hand. One jump along a time line, and one regrouped unit carried or borrowed, are violet, labelled Jump, Carry or Regroup. On a day bar the half from noon until just before midnight is rose, labelled p.m., and the half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline, labelled a.m. The hand, digit, column, jump or date being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open, labelled Place holder, and for nothing else. The hour hand and the minute hand, dials, tick marks, time lines, arrows, operation signs and step labels are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of the content colours, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last run stays shaded on the calendar with its cut, its counts by cells and by the rule, and its answer beside them in green.

writeup.delight: On the first phase, when the count by cells and the count by the rule land on the same number, the two counters flip over together and turn green at once.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet counted. On the first phase one month calendar stands with a start date and an end date set on it in deep blue and no cell shaded. On the second two months stand side by side with a start date in the first and an end date in the second. On the third a month calendar holds a start date and a number of days in deep blue. On the fourth a date is set on the calendar with a violet jump of some days waiting beside it. One thing moves, once: the start date, the first cell of the run or the jump gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any two dates set on the calendar and counted, any run cut at a month end, and any jump of days dragged from a date. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on counting both days, a run across a month end, a finish date and dates some days after.
voiceLines: A calendar with two dates marked, waiting to be counted.
Count the first day and the last day. Then take one date from the other and add one.
Where does the first month end? Count that part, then the rest.
The first day is day one. On which date does the last day fall?
After means add the days. Do you count the first day again?
A new pair of dates. Count them the same way.
Free play. Mark any two dates and count the days between.
Count the cells again. Did you count the first day and the last day?
You counted the days between dates and found a date some days after.

observations.why: the cells include both the first day and the last day, and taking one date from the other leaves one of them out.
observations.soWhat: counting both days, the number of days is the end date minus the start date, then add 1.
observations.observe: The cells counted one by one and the sum taken from the end date agreed once 1 was added.

observations.why: the two months have different numbers of days, so their dates cannot be taken apart as if they were one month.
observations.soWhat: count to the last day of the month first, then on into the next month, and add the two parts.
observations.observe: A run across a month end split into two parts at the last day of the first month.

observations.soWhat: the last day is found by adding to the start date one day fewer than the number of days.
observations.observe: The last day of a course came one day fewer than its number of days after the first day.

observations.why: after means add the days, and the date the jump starts from is not one of them.
observations.soWhat: a fortnight later is 14 days after, and the two kinds of question, how many days and on which date, are kept apart.

source_tool.name: Date Counter
source_tool.blurb: Count the days between two dates on a calendar, both days included, across a month end, find a finish date, and add days or a fortnight to a date.

source_tool.description: A month calendar, or two months side by side when a run crosses a month end, fills the working area, with the last day of the first month marked. A start date is set on it in deep blue, labelled Start, and an end date or a number of days beside it in deep blue, labelled Given. The days between them are shaded as a run of day cells and counted one by one, with a counter that says whether the first day and the last day are included. On the first phase the child counts the cells with both end cells included, then finds the same number by taking the start date from the end date and adding 1, and reads it in green, labelled Answer; a range given as after one date but before another is shaded with both end dates left out. On the second phase the run is cut at the last day of the first month, and its two parts are counted and added. On the third phase a start date and a number of days are set, the start date is day 1, and the last day is marked in green, labelled End. On the fourth phase a violet jump of some days, labelled Jump, is dragged along the calendar from a date, without counting the first day again, and a jump of 14 days stands for a fortnight. The date being counted is amber. The running count at the top left of the canvas counts the days counted.
source_tool.art_direction: Coloured stickers on a wall calendar / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: round clock faces with twelve numbers and sixty small marks, a day bar from midnight to midnight, a time line with jumps, columns of hours, minutes and seconds, and month calendars with seven columns.

Every clock time is written in one notation: 4:15 p.m. for a 12-hour time, with a colon and a.m. or p.m., and 1615 hours for a 24-hour time, four digits and the word hours, never a colon and never a dot. Noon is written 12 noon and midnight 12 midnight. A length of time is written 2 h 15 min, 3 days 5 h and 40 s, or in words, and never as a clock time.

Every hour hand sits at its true angle: it moves on from each number as the minutes pass, so at a quarter past it has gone a quarter of the way to the next number. The minute hand is long, the hour hand short and thick, and the second hand thin, longer than both and vermilion. Label lines stay outside the dial.
A time line that passes 12 midnight shows midnight as its own mark and says the next day after it. A count of days always says whether both the first and the last day are counted.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: hands turning, a jump along a time line, a carried unit moving to the next column, or dates being counted on a calendar.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a digit, a jump or a date the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a time plays in a piece of working: what the question gives, a clock time, a length of time, a start date or a number of days, is deep blue, and what the working reaches, an end time, a length of time, a converted time or a date, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The thin second hand and the seconds it counts are vermilion. One jump along a time line, and one regrouped unit carried or borrowed, is violet. The half of the day from noon until just before midnight is rose on a day bar, and the half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline. The hand, digit, column, jump or date being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open at the front of a 24-hour time. The hour hand and the minute hand are near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Second hand, Jump, Carry, a.m., p.m., Noon and Midnight, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Count the cells again. Did you count the first day and the last day?
voice.onNext: A new pair of dates. Count them the same way.
voice.opening: A calendar with two dates marked, waiting to be counted.
voice.onFinish: You counted the days between dates and found a date some days after.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Mark any two dates and count the days between.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Days after and a fortnight later

placement.where: After the class has marked two dates on a wall calendar and counted the days between them on their fingers. The tool is what counts both days by cells and by the rule, and cuts a run at the month end, which a finger count on a wall calendar can lose.

answer_key.rule: The days from one date to another, counting both days, are the end date minus the start date, then add 1: from 8 September to 16 September, counting both days, is 9 days. Across a month end, count to the last day of the month first, then on into the next month. A finish date is found by adding to the start date one day fewer than the number of days, because the first day is day 1: a 16-day course that begins on 22 November ends 15 days after it, on 7 December. After and a fortnight later add the days to the date without counting the first day again: 25 days after 12 April is 7 May, and a fortnight is 14 days.
answer_key.wrong: The stage keeps the child's count. A count that leaves out the first day or the last stays, and the cell it missed is lit amber. A run across a month end counted with the first month one day short shows the missing cell lit amber. A finish date found by counting the first day twice stays, and the date one day too late is lit amber. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Count both the first day and the last day.
Take the start date from the end date, then add 1.
So from 8 September to 16 September, counting both days, is 9 days.
items.question: A book fair is open from 8 September to 16 September. For how many days is it open?
items.checkpoint: Counting both days, take the start date from the end date, then add 1.
items.misconception: Taking the start date from the end date and stopping there, so the first day is left out.

steps: July has 31 days, so count to the end of July first.
From 27 July to 31 July there are 31 - 27 + 1 = 5 days.
From 1 August to 8 August there are 8 days.
5 + 8 = 13, so from 27 July to 8 August, counting both days, is 13 days.
items.question: A camp runs from 27 July to 8 August. For how many days does it run?
items.checkpoint: Across a month end, count to the last day of the month first, then on into the next month.
items.misconception: Taking 8 from 27 across the two months as if they were one, which gives a negative count.

steps: The first day is day 1, so the last day comes 15 days after it.
Check it: from 22 November to 7 December, counting both days, is 16 days.
So the course ends on 7 December.
items.question: A 16-day course begins on 22 November. On which date does it end?
items.checkpoint: The start date is day 1, so the last day comes one day fewer than the number of days after it.
items.misconception: Counting 16 days on from 22 November, so the course ends a day too late.

steps: After means add the days to the date, without counting the first day again.
April has 30 days, and 30 - 12 = 18, so 18 days after 12 April is 30 April.
25 - 18 = 7, and 7 days after 30 April is 7 May.
So 25 days after 12 April is 7 May.
items.question: A plant is watered on 12 April and again 25 days after. On which date is it watered the second time?
items.checkpoint: After and a fortnight later add the days to the date, and the first day is not counted again.
items.misconception: Counting 12 April as the first of the 25 days, which gives a date one day too early.

items.question: From 2 October to 7 October, counting both days, how many days is that?
From 29 October to 2 November, counting both days, how many days is that?
items.final_answer: 5 days, because 3 days are in October and 2 days are in November

items.question: A 6-day fair begins on 10 October. On which date does it end?
items.final_answer: 15 October, because 5 days after 10 October is 15 October

items.question: What date is 10 days after 6 October?
One person says a visit was after the 6th but before the 11th of a month. Another says it was after the 8th but before the 12th. If both are right, on which dates could the visit be?
items.final_answer: The 9th and the 10th, because those are the dates after the 8th and before the 11th

items.question: From 22 August to 5 September, counting both days, how many days is that?
items.final_answer: 15 days, because 10 days are in August and 5 days are in September

items.question: A 40-day course ended on 10 August. On which date did it begin, counting both days?
items.final_answer: 2 July, because 39 days before 10 August is 2 July

items.question: A jar is filled on 27 October and opened a fortnight later. On which date is it opened?
items.final_answer: 10 November, because 14 days after 27 October is 10 November

student_controls.effect: is set on the calendar in deep blue
is set on the calendar, or the number of days is set beside it
counts the shaded cells and says whether both end days are included
splits a run at the last day of the first month
is dragged along the calendar by some days, or by a fortnight
types a number of days or a date

teaching_notes: Say whether both days are counted every time a number of days is given. To count both days, take the start date from the end date, then add 1. Across a month end, count to the last day of the month first, then on into the next month. After and a fortnight later mean add the days to the date, with the first day not counted again. Where two ranges are given as after one date and before another, list the dates that fit each range and keep the ones they share. Where an answer list gives one day fewer, teach the chapter's own rule of counting both days.
generation_prompt: Build a date counting tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A month calendar, or two months side by side, with the last day of the first month marked. A start date is set in deep blue, labelled Start, and an end date or a number of days beside it, labelled Given; the days between are shaded as a run of cells and counted, with a counter that says whether both end days are included. A Cut handle splits a run at the month end, the last day found is green, labelled End, and a violet jump, labelled Jump, is dragged along the calendar by some days or by a fortnight. The date being counted is amber. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Set the dates on the calendar. Count the cells with both end days, then check by the rule. Drag a jump of days to find a date after.
